That path keeps relying on the existing deadlock retry. - It is guarded by `hasattr(frappe.db, "advisory_lock")`. An older Frappe falls back to a `nullcontext()`, so the Repost Item Valuation isn't marked Failed. 2. **All stock writes for an item-warehouse: `sle_processing_gate(item_code, warehouse)`** in the same file. - `make_sl_entries` and `update_entries_after.__init__` call it. - It takes a transaction-scoped advisory lock, `transaction_advisory_lock(("stock-sle", item_code, warehouse))`. Two workers never pick up the same date/report-type row because each row is claimed with a locking read and a status change. The code is in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/process_period_closing_voucher/process_period_closing_voucher.py`. The work is tracked in the child table `Process Period Closing Voucher Detail`, which has one row per processing date and report type. I read the code but did not run it or test concurrent workers. **How a row is claimed** - `initialize_parallel_threads(docname)` claims up to 4 rows at a time. `schedule_next_date(docname)` claims 1 row at a time. - Both functions select rows with `status = "Queued"` for the parent document. They ordered the rows by `parentfield`, `idx` and `processing_date`. - Both use `.for_update(skip_locked=True)`, which is `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. A row that another transaction has locked is skipped, so two concurrent claimers can't get the same row. - Right after the select, the claimed row's `status` is set to `"Running"`. Because only `Queued` rows are selectable, a `Running` row won't be picked up again. - `schedule_next_date` then calls `frappe.db.commit()` (outside tests) so the lock and status change are released and visible quickly. A comment there says this keeps the transaction short and avoids REPEATABLE READ concurrency errors. - The job is then enqueued with `frappe.enqueue(..., enqueue_after_commit=True)`, so the worker only starts after the `Running` status is committed. **Guard inside the worker** - `process_individual_date(docname, row_name, date, report_type, parentfield)` starts by reading the row's status. If the status isn't `"Running"`, it returns without doing anything. This stops a stale, duplicate or paused job from processing a row. **Recovery** - A row stuck in `Running` can be re-queued: the pause and resume path sets paused rows back to `Queued`, and I saw this around lines 148–186. I did not read that code closely.

Two workers can't process the same date/report-type row because each row is claimed with a locking query and a status flag. The logic is in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/process_period_closing_voucher/process_period_closing_voucher.py`. I read the code but didn't run it. The work is tracked per row in the child table "Process Period Closing Voucher Detail" (PPCVD). Each row is one `processing_date` plus `report_type`, under the parentfields for normal and opening balances. Each row has a `status` of Queued, Running, Completed, Paused or Cancelled. 1. **Claiming rows with a skip-locked query.** Both `initialize_parallel_threads(docname)` and `schedule_next_date(docname)` select rows for the parent where `status == "Queued"`. They order by parentfield, idx and processing_date, and the query ends with `.for_update(skip_locked=True)`. That puts a row-level `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` on the rows they pick, so a concurrent caller skips rows another transaction has locked instead of waiting for them or taking them too. - `initialize_parallel_threads` claims up to 4 rows (`threads = 4`). - `schedule_next_date` claims 1. 2. **Marking the row Running before enqueueing.** While still holding the lock, the claimer calls `frappe.db.set_value(..., "status", "Running")` on each selected row. Only after that does it call `frappe.enqueue(... process_individual_date ..., queue="long", enqueue_after_commit=True, row_name=..., date=..., report_type=..., parentfield=...)`. - In `schedule_next_date` there is also an explicit `frappe.db.commit()` after the status update (skipped in tests). The code comment says this keeps the transaction short and avoids REPEATABLE READ concurrency errors. - The commit releases the lock only after the row is already Running. Any later claimer's `status == "Queued"` filter therefore no longer matches it. 3. **A check inside the worker.** `process_individual_date` starts by re-reading that row's status. If the status is not "Running", it returns without doing anything. This protects against rows that were paused or cancelled, or are otherwise stale, between enqueueing and execution. 4. **Handing off to the next date.** When a worker finishes, it saves `closing_balance` and sets the row's status to "Completed". It commits that, then calls `schedule_next_date`, which claims the next Queued row with the same locking pattern. 5. **The final summary step.** When no Queued rows remain and every row is Completed, `schedule_next_date` enqueues `summarize_and_post_ledger_entries`. It guards that call with `is_job_running(f"summarize_{docname}")` and a `job_name`, so the summary isn't enqueued twice either. Pausing, resuming and cancelling use the same status column. `pause_pcv_processing` and `resume_pcv_processing` flip rows between Queued/Running and Paused, and `cancel_pcv_processing` sets Queued rows to Cancelled. The Running-status check in step 3 is what stops a paused or cancelled row from being processed by a job that was already enqueued.

That returns an empty result unless both of these hold: - A Work Order Operation on that Work Order has `finished_good == item_code`, meaning the item is a semi-finished good produced by an earlier operation. - The item has serial numbers or batches enabled (`has_serial_no` or `has_batch_no`). 3. **Produced minus consumed.** Both sets are built from submitted Stock Entries of the same Work Order, using the Serial and Batch Entry rows of each bundle (via `_get_operation_bundles` and `_get_operation_sn_batch`): - **Produced:** bundles on "Manufacture" entries where the row is a finished item and `t_warehouse` equals the source warehouse. - **Consumed:** bundles on rows of the same item whose `s_warehouse` equals that warehouse. - **Serial numbers:** those produced and not yet consumed. - **Batches:** per-batch quantity of produced minus consumed, kept only where it is greater than 0. 4. **Capping to the row qty.** `_cap_pool_to_qty` trims the pool to the row's quantity: - **Serial numbers:** it takes the first `int(qty)` of the available list. - **Batches:** it walks the available batches in order, taking `min(batch_qty, remaining)` from each until the quantity is met. 5. **Bundle creation.** `SerialBatchCreation(...).make_serial_and_batch_bundle()` builds an Outward Serial and Batch Bundle with `do_not_submit=True`, so it is left as a draft. Its name is set on `row.serial_and_batch_bundle` and `use_serial_batch_fields` is set to 0. **If fewer units are available than the row's qty.** It fills only what exists. Serial numbers are sliced to however many are available, and batches are taken up to their available quantities. The row's `qty` is not reduced, and no error is raised. The shortfall is left unassigned for the user to fill in manually, as the function's docstring says. If nothing is available, no bundle is created and the row stays blank.

The item must be the `finished_good` of some Work Order Operation on that Work Order. That is what makes it a semi-finished good. 2. The item must have serial numbers or batches enabled. 3. It collects what was produced: serials and batch quantities from submitted Stock Entries of that Work Order where the item went into this warehouse as the target (`t_warehouse`). For serials, any serial not already consumed is kept. **Mechanism: database savepoints.** The code calls `frappe.db.savepoint("<name>")` just before the optional write. If the write fails, it calls `frappe.db.rollback(save_point="<name>")` inside the `except`. I read two of these call sites in full (`stock/utils.py` and the Purchase Order mapper). The rest I identified only from `savepoint(` grep hits and comments, without reading each handler. **Why it is needed.** On PostgreSQL, a failed statement such as a duplicate-key INSERT puts the whole transaction into an aborted state. Every later statement then fails until a rollback is issued. A savepoint lets the code roll back only the failed statement, and the transaction stays usable. The code comments say this directly: "preserve transaction in postgres" in `stock/utils.py`, and "savepoint so a failed insert doesn't poison the transaction on postgres" in `plaid_settings.py`. **How it differs from a full rollback.** - A plain `frappe.db.rollback()` discards the entire transaction. That includes the parent document being submitted and any earlier work, and it also drops any pending commit hooks and similar state. - `rollback(save_point=...)` undoes only the work done since the savepoint. The outer work is kept and the caller carries on. - The comments in `opening_invoice_creation_tool.py` and `frappe_crm_api.py` say the same thing. A failure there should not discard the Customer just created or the other invoices, which a full rollback would lose on Postgres. **Where it is applied.** - **`erpnext/stock/utils.py`, `_create_bin`:** it creates the Bin under savepoint `create_bin`. On `UniqueValidationError` (a concurrent insert) it rolls back to the savepoint and then fetches the existing Bin with `get_last_doc`. - **`erpnext/buying/doctype/purchase_order/mapper.py`:** it submits the auto-created Subcontracting Order under savepoint `submit_subcontracting_order`. On failure it rolls back to the savepoint and adds a "Submit Action Failed" comment to the document. - **`erpnext/subcontracting/doctype/subcontracting_receipt/mapper.py`:** it uses the same pattern, with savepoint `submit_subcontracting_receipt`. - **`erpnext/accounts/doctype/fiscal_year/fiscal_year.py`:** it auto-creates a Fiscal Year under savepoint `auto_create_fiscal_year`, so a duplicate-year insert does not abort the transaction. - **`erpnext/accounts/doctype/payment_entry/payment_entry.py`:** the subscription update uses savepoint `subscription_update`. - **`erpnext/stock/reorder_item.py`:** the auto-created Material Request uses savepoint `reorder_mr`. - **`erpnext/crm/frappe_crm_api.py`:** the address and contact links use savepoints `crm_create_address` and `crm_customer_links`. - ERPNext uses database savepoints. The pattern is `frappe.db.savepoint(name)` before the risky write. If the write fails, the code calls `frappe.db.rollback(save_point=name)`. **How it differs from a full rollback** - A plain `frappe.db.rollback()` discards the whole transaction. That includes the parent document, such as the submitting doc or the Customer, and any earlier rows in a batch. - `rollback(save_point=...)` undoes only the work done since that savepoint. On PostgreSQL it also clears the "current transaction is aborted" state, so later statements work again. The rest of the transaction stays intact and can still be committed. - MariaDB doesn't abort the transaction on a failed statement, so this problem only shows up on PostgreSQL. The code comments say as much, for example `# preserve transaction in postgres` in `stock/utils.py`. - `.github/POSTGRES_COMPATIBILITY.md` (section 5, "Transaction / runtime") and the checker `.github/helper/postgres_compat.py` mention "savepoint discipline" as a review concern. **Mechanism:** the codebase uses database savepoints. The pattern is `frappe.db.savepoint(name)` before the risky write. If the write fails, the code calls `frappe.db.rollback(save_point=name)`. The savepoint API is Frappe's, and I did not open its source. I only read the ERPNext call sites listed below, so the savepoint SQL behaviour described here is the standard PostgreSQL behaviour, not something I confirmed in Frappe. **How it differs from a full rollback:** - A plain `frappe.db.rollback()` discards the whole transaction. That includes the parent document being submitted, earlier loop iterations, and any queued or after-commit hooks. - `rollback(save_point=…)` undoes only the work done since that savepoint. PostgreSQL aborts the entire transaction after any failed statement ("current transaction is aborted…"). Rolling back to the savepoint clears that aborted state, so later statements in the same transaction work again. - The parent work and previously completed work are kept. - MariaDB doesn't have this poisoning problem. The savepoints are what make the same code behave correctly on Postgres. **Where it is applied:** - `erpnext/stock/utils.py`, `_create_bin`: a savepoint around `Bin.insert()`. final answer
ERPNext doesn't use `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` anywhere in its Python code (I searched for those keywords and found none). It controls NULL ordering in two other ways, both written with the Frappe query builder (`frappe.qb`), so they work the same on MariaDB and PostgreSQL. **1. An `IS NULL` flag as the first sort key** `erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py`, in `get_item_price()`, picks a single Item Price row with `.limit(1)`. The sort is: - `.orderby(ip.valid_from.isnull(), order=asc)`. A boolean `IS NULL` sorts 0 before 1 on both databases. Rows with a `valid_from` therefore come first and rows with a NULL `valid_from` come last. - `.orderby(ip.valid_from, order=desc)`. This picks the latest valid-from date among the dated rows. Without the flag, MariaDB would put NULLs first in `ASC` order and last in `DESC`. PostgreSQL does the opposite, so a different price could win. **2. Wrapping the sort key in `IfNull` or `Coalesce` with a sentinel value** The NULL is replaced by a fixed value, so it sorts the same way on both databases. - **`get_item_price()` (`get_item_details.py`)**: - `IfNull(ip.batch_no, "")` descending. - `IfNull(ip.customer, "")` descending, when a customer is given. - `IfNull(ip.supplier, "")` descending, when a supplier is given. - These make a specific batch, customer or supplier price beat a generic one, because `""` sorts below any real value. The `.limit(1)` makes this a row-picking decision. The same function's date filter also uses `IfNull(ip.valid_from, "2000-01-01")` and `IfNull(ip.valid_upto, "2500-12-31")`. - **`erpnext/controllers/queries.py` (line ~914)**: `IfNull(bin_dt.actual_qty, 0)` descending, so items with no Bin row are treated as zero stock. - **`erpnext/accounts/doctype/payment_entry/payment_entry.py` (line ~2798)**: `Coalesce(PR.transaction_date, PR.creation)` ascending. This falls back to `creation` for payment requests without a transaction date. - **`erpnext/setup/doctype/email_digest/email_digest.py` (line ~239)**: `IfNull(todo.date, "1000-01-01")`. The code comment says "NULL dates first, as MariaDB `date asc` did". This is the clearest case of keeping MariaDB's behaviour on PostgreSQL. - **`erpnext/www/payment_setup_certification.py`, `get_all_certifications_of_a_member()`**: `IfNull(cc.to_date, "0001-01-01")` descending. NULL (an open-ended certification) sorts last.

ERPNext has no `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` anywhere. A grep for those keywords and the `nulls_first`/`nulls_last` query-builder variants found nothing. It controls NULL ordering in three other ways. I found the three query sites below by searching, so there may be others I didn't find. **1. A leading `IS NULL` sort key, so NULLs sort last on both engines** - `get_serial_nos_based_on_filters` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/serial_and_batch_bundle/serial_and_batch_bundle.py` (around line 2510) picks serial numbers in FIFO or expiry order and applies a `LIMIT`. - When `order_by == "amc_expiry_date"` (and it isn't LIFO), it first adds `orderby(order_by_column.isnull(), order=Order.desc)`. This puts NULL rows last on both engines. - It then adds `orderby(order_by_column)`. - Without this, MariaDB would put NULL-expiry serials first and Postgres would put them last. That would change which serials the `LIMIT` returns. **2. A sentinel value through `IfNull`, which reproduces MariaDB's NULLs-first order** - `EmailDigest.get_todo_list` in `erpnext/setup/doctype/email_digest/email_digest.py` (around lines 225–243) takes the first 20 open ToDos. - Its priority sort is a `Case` expression with `else_(0)`. This matches MySQL `FIELD()` returning 0 for NULL or unknown priority, so those rows come first. - The date sort is `orderby(IfNull(todo.date, "1000-01-01"))`. A very early sentinel date keeps NULL dates first on both engines, as MariaDB's `date asc` did. - `test_get_todo_list_priority_and_date_ordering` in `erpnext/setup/doctype/email_digest/test_email_digest.py` checks both behaviours. It fails if either sentinel is flipped. **3. Filtering NULLs out, so the first row is never a NULL one** - In `erpnext/crm/report/lead_conversion_time/lead_conversion_time.py` (around lines 119–127), `first_contact` takes the first Communication row, ordered by `communication_date`, with `limit(1)`. - It adds `.where(... & comm.communication_date.isnotnull())` and checks that a row came back before reading `[0][0]`. - Before this guard, MariaDB (NULLs first) returned a NULL-dated row, giving a wrong duration. Postgres returned the earliest real date. - `test_first_contact_ignores_null_communication_date` in `test_lead_conversion_time.py` covers it. Many other `isnotnull()` calls in the codebase are plain filters, not ordering fixes.

final answer
ERPNext doesn't use `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` anywhere in Python. I grepped `*.py` for those keywords and found no matches. Instead, it makes NULL placement the same on both databases by changing the query itself. There are three mechanisms. I read the code at four of the sites below. I only saw the email digest one as a grep hit, so I haven't checked it in context. **1. Coalesce the nullable column with `IfNull(col, sentinel)` in `ORDER BY`.** NULL then sorts as a known value, so both databases agree on where it lands. - `erpnext/setup/doctype/email_digest/email_digest.py:239` orders ToDos with `.orderby(IfNull(todo.date, "1000-01-01"))`. The inline comment says "NULL dates first, as MariaDB `date asc` did". This matters because the digest takes the first rows. The related test is `test_get_todo_list_priority_and_date_ordering`. - `erpnext/www/payment_setup_certification.py:24` (`get_all_certifications_of_a_member`) uses `.orderby(IfNull(cc.to_date, "0001-01-01"), order=desc)`. A NULL `to_date` sorts as the earliest date, so it comes last in descending order. That is MariaDB's behaviour. - `erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py:1235-1255` picks the best Item Price with `LIMIT 1` (the function around line 1224). It orders by `IfNull(ip.batch_no, "")`, `IfNull(ip.customer, "")` and `IfNull(ip.supplier, "")`, all descending. Rows with a value therefore beat NULL or empty ones on both databases. - `erpnext/controllers/queries.py:914` orders by `IfNull(bin_dt.actual_qty, 0)` descending. **2. Add an explicit `col IS NULL` sort key before the real sort key.** This is in `erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py:1233`: `.orderby(ip.valid_from.isnull(), order=asc)` followed by `.orderby(ip.valid_from, order=desc)`. The boolean `IS NULL` is 0 for rows with a date and 1 for NULL rows. Ascending order therefore puts rows with a `valid_from` first, and NULL rows last. It then breaks ties by latest `valid_from`. Because the query has `LIMIT 1`, this decides which price is returned. **3. Filter NULLs out so they can't be the first row.** In `erpnext/crm/report/lead_conversion_time/lead_conversion_time.py:119-126`, the first-contact query uses `.where(comm.communication_date.isnotnull())`, then `.orderby(comm.communication_date).limit(1)`. A NULL `communication_date` can't win on PostgreSQL, where NULLs sort last. The test `test_first_contact_ignores_null_communication_date` covers this. A related case is a test named "NULL and empty-string `tax_withholding_group` must be treated as the same value". It treats NULL and empty string as equal, but it is about equality, not ordering.

ERPNext doesn't use `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST`. A grep for those keywords found nothing. It makes NULL ordering engine-independent by adding an explicit sort key in front of, or in place of, the nullable column. I found these query sites with grep. I did not trace every possible ORDER BY, so the list may be incomplete. **Mechanism 1: a leading `IS NULL` sort key** The code orders by `col.isnull()` first and by the column itself second. - MariaDB treats NULL as the smallest value. PostgreSQL treats it as the largest. - The boolean `col IS NULL` is false (0) for real values and true (1) for NULL. It sorts the same way on both engines. - `.isnull()` ascending puts NULLs last, and descending puts them first. Concrete sites: - **`erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py`, around line 1132:** this is the Item Price lookup. It orders by `ip.valid_from.isnull()` ascending, then `valid_from` descending, then `creation` descending. Dated prices win over undated ones, and the newest date wins. - **`erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py`, around line 1233:** this is the Item Price lookup with `limit(1)`, so the sort decides which price is returned. It uses the same `valid_from.isnull()` ascending then `valid_from` descending pair. It then orders by `IfNull(batch_no, "")` descending and `uom` descending. - **`erpnext/selling/page/point_of_sale/point_of_sale.py`, around line 234:** this is the POS item price query. It orders by `ItemPrice.valid_from.isnull()` ascending, then `valid_from` descending. - **`erpnext/stock/doctype/serial_and_batch_bundle/serial_and_batch_bundle.py`, around line 2511:** when the order is by `amc_expiry_date` (FIFO/FEFO), it orders by `order_by_column.isnull()` descending, then by the column. This is the opposite polarity to the price queries. Its effect is to put NULLs first. **Mechanism 2: `IfNull` or `Coalesce` with a sentinel value** NULL is replaced by a fixed value that sorts the same way on both engines. - **`erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py`, around lines 1235, 1250 and 1255:** `IfNull(ip.batch_no, "")`, `IfNull(ip.customer, "")` and `IfNull(ip.supplier, "")` are all ordered descending. Rows with a specific batch, customer or supplier beat generic rows. - **`erpnext/www/payment_setup_certification.py`, line 24:** `IfNull(cc.to_date, "0001-01-01")` descending puts NULL dates last. - **`erpnext/setup/doctype/email_digest/email_digest.py`, line 239:** `IfNull(todo.date, "1000-01-01")`. The comment says "NULL dates first, as MariaDB `date asc` did". The code deliberately reproduces MariaDB's behaviour on PostgreSQL, and this one is under a `limit(20)`. - **`erpnext/accounts/doctype/payment_entry/payment_entry.py`, around line 2798:** `Coalesce(PR.transaction_date, PR.creation)` ascending decides the order in which Payment Requests are allocated. A second key, `PR.creation`, follows with the comment "unique tiebreaker ... same order on both engines". - **`erpnext/accounts/doctype/pricing_rule/utils.py`, around line 155:** the raw SQL has `order by coalesce(\`tabPricing Rule\`.priority, '') desc, name desc`. A NULL priority is treated as an empty string, so it ranks below any set priority. - **`erpnext/controllers/queries.py`, around line 914:** `IfNull(bin_dt.actual_qty, 0)` descending, then warehouse. A missing Bin row counts as zero stock. The code also adds deterministic tiebreakers (`creation` and `name`). Rows with equal or NULL keys then come out in the same order on both databases.

ERPNext has no `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` clause anywhere in the code (I searched the Python files). Instead, it makes NULL ordering engine-independent in three ways. The stated rule is that MariaDB's behaviour is the reference and PostgreSQL is made to match it. That rule is written in `.greptile/config.json`. I read the sites below directly. I did not read `lead_conversion_time.py` itself, only its test and docstring, so the filter there is as the test describes it. **1. Sort on a boolean `IS NULL` expression first, then on the column** - Site: `get_serial_nos_based_on_filters` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/serial_and_batch_bundle/serial_and_batch_bundle.py`, around lines 2507–2512. - This query picks serial numbers with a `LIMIT` (`kwargs.qty`), so the sort decides which serials are selected. - For the non-LIFO case with `order_by == "amc_expiry_date"`, it adds `.orderby(order_by_column.isnull(), order=Order.desc)` and then `.orderby(order_by_column)`. - `IS NULL` evaluates to 1 for NULL rows, so descending order puts them first on both engines. That reproduces MariaDB's NULLs-first behaviour for ascending sorts. **2. Replace NULL with a sentinel value using `IfNull`/`COALESCE` inside the `ORDER BY`** - `EmailDigest.get_todo_list` in `erpnext/setup/doctype/email_digest/email_digest.py` (lines 225–243). The query has `LIMIT 20`, so ordering decides which to-dos are included. - `.orderby(IfNull(todo.date, "1000-01-01"))` has the comment "NULL dates first, as MariaDB `date asc` did". - A `Case()` expression for priority ends in `.else_(0)`. It emulates MySQL `FIELD(priority,'High','Medium','Low')`, where NULL, empty or unknown values give 0 and sort first. - `test_get_todo_list_priority_and_date_ordering` in `test_email_digest.py` fails if either sentinel is flipped. - `get_all_certifications_of_a_member` in `erpnext/www/payment_setup_certification.py` (line 24) uses `.orderby(IfNull(cc.to_date, "0001-01-01"), order=desc)`. This pins NULL to the oldest position, so it sorts last in a descending sort on both engines. It is the same technique used in the other direction. - `erpnext/controllers/queries.py` (line 914) uses `.orderby(IfNull(bin_dt.actual_qty, 0), order=Order.desc)`. This treats NULL as 0 instead of leaving it to the engine. **3. Remove NULLs from the candidate set so ordering can't pick them** - Site: the `lead_conversion_time` report in `erpnext/crm/report/lead_conversion_time/`. - It computes `first_contact` by ordering on `communication_date` and reading `row[0][0]`. - Without a guard, MariaDB (NULLs first) returned a NULL-dated `Communication`, which gave a wrong duration. PostgreSQL (NULLs last) returned the earliest real date. - The fix, as described in `test_first_contact_ignores_null_communication_date`, filters `communication_date IS NOT NULL` and guards the slice. Both engines then use the earliest real date. The test expects a duration of 22 days.

ERPNext doesn't use `NULLS FIRST` / `NULLS LAST` anywhere. A grep over the `.py` files found no `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` clause. Instead it controls NULL placement in three ways, all portable across MariaDB and PostgreSQL. **1. A leading `col IS NULL` sort key** This is a boolean sort key placed before the real sort column. MariaDB and PostgreSQL both sort `false` before `true`, so ascending puts non-NULL rows first and descending puts NULL rows first. - `erpnext/selling/page/point_of_sale/point_of_sale.py` (item price lookup, around lines 232–235): the query filters on `valid_from`/`valid_upto` and then does `.orderby(ItemPrice.valid_from.isnull(), order=Order.asc).orderby(ItemPrice.valid_from, order=Order.desc)`. The newest dated price wins, and open-ended prices with a NULL `valid_from` sort last. Without this, PostgreSQL's NULLs-first behaviour on a descending sort would pick the undated row. - `erpnext/stock/doctype/serial_and_batch_bundle/serial_and_batch_bundle.py`, `get_serial_nos_based_on_filters` (around lines 2507–2512): for FIFO picking ordered by `amc_expiry_date`, it adds `.orderby(order_by_column.isnull(), order=Order.desc)` before `.orderby(order_by_column)`. NULL-expiry serial numbers are therefore always picked first, matching MariaDB's ascending NULLs-first order. The query uses `LIMIT qty` and `FOR UPDATE`, so this decides which serial numbers get picked. **2. Replacing NULL with a sentinel value in the sort key** - `erpnext/setup/doctype/email_digest/email_digest.py`, `EmailDigest.get_todo_list`: it orders by `IfNull(todo.date, "1000-01-01")`, with a comment saying "NULL dates first, as MariaDB `date asc` did". It also uses a `Case().when(priority == "High", 1) ... .else_(0)` expression to reproduce MySQL's `field(priority, ...)` behaviour, where NULL or unknown priority sorts first. A final `.orderby(todo.name)` breaks ties. This query uses `.limit(20)`, so the ordering decides which to-dos make it into the digest. `test_email_digest.py::test_get_todo_list_priority_and_date_ordering` covers it. **3. Filtering NULLs out when the code takes the first row** - `erpnext/crm/report/lead_conversion_time/lead_conversion_time.py` (around lines 121–123): the first-contact query orders by `comm.communication_date` and reads the first row. It now adds `comm.communication_date.isnotnull()` to the `where` clause. MariaDB (NULLs first) would otherwise return a NULL-dated Communication and a wrong duration, while PostgreSQL (NULLs last) returned the earliest real date. `test_lead_conversion_time.py::test_first_contact_ignores_null_communication_date` checks that both engines agree. A related query is `erpnext/controllers/queries.py` around line 914, which uses `orderby(IfNull(bin_dt.actual_qty, 0), order=Order.desc)`. This is the same `IfNull` approach, so NULL quantities sort as 0.

final answer
**Short answer: only partly.** A Stock Entry does have a validation that throws on an expired batch. It doesn't run for plain Material Issue or Material Transfer entries, which are the cases you asked about. **The check that exists** - `StockEntryDetail.validate_batch()` is in `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_entry_detail/stock_entry_detail.py`, around lines 88–99. - It throws "Batch {0} of Item {1} has expired." when `getdate(parent_doc.posting_date) > getdate(Batch.expiry_date)`. - It also throws if the batch is disabled. - The comparison uses the Stock Entry's posting date, not today's date. **Why it misses Issue and Transfer** - `StockEntry.validate_batch()` is in `stock_entry.py` at line 1479 and is called from `validate()` at line 310. - It only calls the row-level check when `purpose` is one of "Material Transfer for Manufacture", "Manufacture", "Repack" or "Send to Subcontractor". - "Material Issue" and "Material Transfer" are not in that list, so those rows are never checked. **The ledger-level check doesn't cover it either** - `StockLedgerEntry.validate_batch()` is in `stock_ledger_entry.py`, lines 287–299, and is called at line 92. It has a similar expiry throw. - It is skipped when `voucher_type == "Stock Entry"`, so it never applies to Stock Entries. **What does cover Material Issue and Material Transfer** - Batch pickers filter out expired batches rather than throwing: - `serial_and_batch_bundle.py` has `get_non_expired_batches` and `expiry_date >= today()` filters in its batch queries, around lines 2570–2580, 3173 and 3518. - `serial_no.py` filters the batch query on expiry at around line 288. - `pick_list.py` excludes expired batches at around line 299. - A user who enters an expired batch by hand, or whose batch expires after selection, is not stopped at submit by any validation I found for these two purposes. I searched `erpnext/stock` for expiry checks and found no other throw. - I did not trace the Serial and Batch Bundle submit path in full. I only grepped it for "expired" and found no throw there.

I read the code but did not run it. **What I found** 1. `StockEntry.validate_batch` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_entry/stock_entry.py` (around line 1479) is called from `validate` (line 310). - It only runs for the purposes "Material Transfer for Manufacture", "Manufacture", "Repack" and "Send to Subcontractor". - For those purposes it calls `StockEntryDetail.validate_batch` in `stock_entry_detail/stock_entry_detail.py`. - That method throws "Batch {0} of Item {1} has expired." if the batch's `expiry_date` is earlier than the Stock Entry's `posting_date`. It also throws if the batch is disabled. - Plain "Material Issue" and "Material Transfer" are not in that list. 2. `StockLedgerEntry.validate_batch` in `stock_ledger_entry.py` throws the same "has expired" error. It is explicitly guarded by `voucher_type != "Stock Entry"`, so it never fires for Stock Entries. 3. The serial and batch bundle check is in `validate_serialized_batch` in `erpnext/stock/services/serial_batch_bundle_service.py` (lines 106–147). It throws `BatchExpiredError` with "Row #{0}: The batch {1} has already expired." when the batch expiry is before the posting date. The code sets `is_material_issue = True` for Stock Entry purposes "Material Issue" and "Material Transfer", then does `continue`, which skips the expiry check for those rows. This check does cover other Stock Entry purposes, such as Material Receipt, and other doctypes. **What does limit expired batches in the UI** - The batch pickers in `serial_and_batch_bundle.py` filter out expired batches. They use `expiry_date >= today() or expiry_date is null`, around lines 3173 and 3518. - `stock_entry/services/serial_batch.py` has `get_expired_batches` and `get_expired_batch_items`, which look up expired batches. - Pick List has its own hard check, `PickList.validate_expired_batches`. These are selection filters and helpers, not a submit-time block. A user can still pick an expired batch manually in a Material Issue or Material Transfer, and I found no submit-time validation that would reject it.

**No. ERPNext has no submit-time check that blocks an expired batch on a Stock Entry.** The one hard validation that exists explicitly skips Stock Entries. The rest only hides expired batches from the picker. **The hard check skips Stock Entries.** `StockLedgerEntry.validate_batch()` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/stock_ledger_entry.py` (around lines 287–299) is the only place that throws "Batch {0} of Item {1} has expired." It throws when the posting date is later than the batch's `expiry_date`. It is guarded by `if self.batch_no and self.voucher_type != "Stock Entry":`, so Stock Entry vouchers never reach the throw. Delivery Note and Sales Invoice (outgoing) and Purchase Receipt and Purchase Invoice (incoming) can still hit it. It also skips Purchase Receipt and Purchase Invoice returns, and Delivery Note and Sales Invoice returns. **Batches now live on the Serial and Batch Bundle.** I found no `expiry_date` validation in `erpnext/stock/doctype/serial_and_batch_bundle/serial_and_batch_bundle.py`. A grep of that file for "has expired", `validate_batch` and `expiry` turned up only the picker queries below. The new bundle flow doesn't always set `batch_no` on the ledger entry either, so I didn't verify whether `validate_batch()` is reached for bundle-based vouchers at all. **Expired batches are only filtered out of selection.** The same file's batch-fetching queries (around lines 2580, 3173 and 3518) add `expiry_date >= today() OR expiry_date IS NULL`. Auto-fetch and the batch picker therefore don't offer expired batches. The Available Batch report (`erpnext/stock/report/available_batch_report/available_batch_report.py`, line 169) applies a similar filter. This is a UI and query filter, not a submit-time validation. A user can still enter or retain an expired batch manually and submit. **Reporting only.** The Batch Item Expiry Status report (`erpnext/stock/report/batch_item_expiry_status`) lists batches and their days to expiry but doesn't block anything. I didn't search outside `erpnext/stock` for other validations.

**Only partly.** ERPNext does throw "Batch {0} of Item {1} has expired." for an expired batch, but a Stock Entry only triggers it for four purposes. Plain Material Issue and Material Transfer are not checked. The check also runs on `validate`, which happens on save and again on submit, not in a separate submit-only hook. **Where the check exists** - `StockEntryDetail.validate_batch()` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_entry_detail/stock_entry_detail.py:88-99` does the work. - It returns early if the row has no `batch_no`. - It throws if the batch is disabled. - It throws `Batch {0} of Item {1} has expired.` if `getdate(parent_doc.posting_date) > getdate(Batch.expiry_date)`. - The comparison is against the Stock Entry's posting date, not today's date. - `StockEntry.validate()` calls `self.validate_batch()` (`stock_entry.py:310`). - `StockEntry.validate_batch()` (`stock_entry.py:1479`) only loops over the item rows for these purposes: - Material Transfer for Manufacture - Manufacture - Repack - Send to Subcontractor **Where it doesn't apply** - Material Issue and ordinary Material Transfer are not in that list. `StockEntry.validate_batch()` never calls the row check for them, so I found no expiry check on the Stock Entry itself for those purposes. - The Stock Ledger Entry validation is the other place that might catch it. `StockLedgerEntry.validate_batch()` (`stock_ledger_entry.py:287`) has an equivalent expiry check, but it begins with `if self.batch_no and self.voucher_type != "Stock Entry"`. Stock Entries are therefore skipped there too. - Batches are now usually selected through a Serial and Batch Bundle. The explicit rejection of expired batches that I found in that code is in the helpers that build the picking lists. `get_non_expired_batches` and the `expiry_date >= today() OR NULL` query filters (`serial_and_batch_bundle.py` around lines 2570, 3173 and 3518) hide expired batches from auto-selection. That is a filter on suggestions, not a submit-time throw. - I didn't trace whether the Serial and Batch Bundle's own validation rejects an expired batch that is entered manually. I only grepped `erpnext/stock` for expiry handling. **Conclusion:** a user can issue or transfer an expired batch with a Stock Entry of purpose Material Issue or Material Transfer. Only Manufacture, Repack, Material Transfer for Manufacture and Send to Subcontractor block it.

**Partly. ERPNext has no general expired-batch check for Stock Entries. The only submit-time throw covers a few purposes, and it checks the legacy `batch_no` field on the row, not the batches inside a Serial and Batch Bundle.** **What exists** - `StockEntry.validate()` calls `self.validate_batch()` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_entry/stock_entry.py`, around line 310, with the method at about line 1479). - That method only calls `item.validate_batch()` on each row when `purpose` is one of `Material Transfer for Manufacture`, `Manufacture`, `Repack` or `Send to Subcontractor`. - `StockEntryDetail.validate_batch()` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_entry_detail/stock_entry_detail.py`, about lines 88–99) does two things: - It throws "Batch {0} of Item {1} is disabled." if the batch is disabled. - It throws "Batch {0} of Item {1} has expired." if the Stock Entry's `posting_date` is later than the batch's `expiry_date`. **What is not covered** - **Material Issue and Material Transfer:** These are the purposes you asked about, and they are not in the list above. `StockEntry.validate_batch()` therefore never runs the expiry check for them. - **Stock Ledger Entry:** `StockLedgerEntry.validate_batch()` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/stock_ledger_entry.py`, about lines 287–299) has the same "has expired" throw. It explicitly skips it when `voucher_type == "Stock Entry"`. It only applies to other vouchers such as Delivery Note and Purchase Receipt. - **Serial and Batch Bundle:** I found no expiry-date throw in `serial_and_batch_bundle.py`. Expiry only appears there as a filter (about lines 3173 and 3518, plus `get_non_expired_batches`) that hides expired batches when batches are auto-picked or listed. It does not block a batch that was entered manually. **Other expiry handling** - `stock_entry.js` sets an `include_expired_batches` filter at about line 130, so the batch picker can show expired batches. - `serial_batch.get_expired_batch_items` is a helper behind a UI button that lists expired batches that still have stock. - `PickList.validate_expired_batches` does throw "The following batches are expired…", but that is on Pick List, not Stock Entry. **Summary:** A plain Material Issue or Material Transfer with an expired batch is not blocked by an expiry validation. It is only discouraged by hiding expired batches in the pickers and auto-selection. The one hard block is the manufacturing, repack and subcontract set, and it only reads the legacy `batch_no` field.

final answer
No. Purchase Order has no automatic spend-limit check against the supplier. I found no `check_credit_limit` in `purchase_order.py` and no credit-limit field for suppliers in the buying module. **Sales side, for comparison** - `SalesOrder.check_credit_limit` in `selling/doctype/sales_order/sales_order.py` calls `check_credit_limit()` in `selling/doctype/customer/customer.py`. - That function compares the customer's outstanding balance, plus open orders and the new amount, against a monetary limit. The limit is stored per company on the Customer. - Delivery Note, Sales Invoice and Journal Entry have their own `check_credit_limit` methods. **What gates Purchase Order submission** - `PurchaseOrder.validate_supplier()` in `buying/doctype/purchase_order/purchase_order.py` (line 272) is called from `validate`, which runs on save and therefore before submit. - It reads two flags on the Supplier: `prevent_pos` and `warn_pos`. - If `prevent_pos` is set, it throws an error that Purchase Orders are not allowed for the supplier because of its scorecard standing. - If `warn_pos` is set, it shows an orange "Caution" message but still lets the order through. - The Supplier Scorecard sets these flags. `buying/doctype/supplier_scorecard/supplier_scorecard.py` copies them from the matching scorecard standing, which are the Supplier Scorecard Standing rows. Each standing has `prevent_pos`, `warn_pos`, `prevent_rfqs` and `warn_rfqs`. - Request for Quotation has a similar check on `prevent_rfqs` in `validate_supplier_list`. - Separately, a Supplier's `on_hold` and `hold_type` fields block invoices or payments. Those checks apply to Purchase Invoice and Payment Entry, not to Purchase Order creation. **How this differs from a credit limit** - **Basis:** a credit limit is a quantitative financial exposure check. It compares the amount owed against a set number. The Purchase Order gate is a qualitative performance check. It is a boolean flag that comes from the supplier's scorecard standing, such as Poor or Average, and ignores the order value and the outstanding payables. - **Direction:** a credit limit protects you from the customer's credit risk. The scorecard gate protects you from supplier quality and reliability risk. - **Override:** the credit limit can be bypassed by a role (`credit_controller`) or by the "bypass credit limit check at Sales Order" setting. The Purchase Order flag is a block or a warning, with no role-based override in that code.

final answer
**No. Purchase Order has no automatic spend-limit check against the supplier.** I searched the buying code and found no credit-limit equivalent on the supplier side. I did not open the Sales Order credit-limit code, so the comparison below is from general knowledge of ERPNext and not from this repo. **What does gate Purchase Order submission** The gate is `PurchaseOrder.validate_supplier()` in `erpnext/buying/doctype/purchase_order/purchase_order.py`, around lines 272-294. `PurchaseOrder.validate()` calls it, so it runs on save and therefore before submit. It is a Supplier Scorecard standing check: - **Block:** if the Supplier has `prevent_pos` set, it looks up the supplier's Supplier Scorecard `status`. If a standing exists, it calls `frappe.throw("Purchase Orders are not allowed for {supplier} due to a scorecard standing of {standing}")`. - **Warn:** if the Supplier has `warn_pos` set, it only calls `frappe.msgprint` with a "Caution" message (orange indicator). The order is not blocked. **Where the flags come from** - The Supplier Scorecard (`supplier_scorecard.py`) scores the supplier from weighted criteria over scorecard periods. - `SupplierScorecard.update_standing()` and `apply_standing()` map that score to a standing band. - Each band is a Supplier Scorecard Standing, which carries `warn_pos`, `prevent_pos`, `warn_rfqs`, `prevent_rfqs` and notify options. These flags end up on the supplier. **How it differs from a credit limit** | | Customer credit limit (Sales Order) | Purchase Order scorecard gate | |---|---|---| | What it measures | A monetary exposure cap. In ERPNext this is the customer's outstanding balance plus open orders, compared to a configured amount. | Supplier performance quality, a weighted score across the scorecard criteria. | | Direction | Protects the company from lending risk, which is receivables owed to it. | Protects the company from supplier unreliability. | | Trigger | Amount-based: the check depends on the order value and the running balance. | Status-based: a standing is reached and the flag is on. The PO amount and spend to date are not considered. | | Control | Configured amounts per customer, with an override role. | Boolean flags per standing band, with no money threshold. It can be a hard block or only a warning. | | Dependency | Works from ledger and order data. | Depends on the scorecard having been computed. If the supplier has no scorecard status, `prevent_pos` has no effect. | The scorecard gate is therefore a qualitative, performance-based hold on a supplier and not a limit on how much you may spend with them.

**No. Purchase Order has no automatic spend-limit check against a supplier.** I found no purchase-side equivalent of the customer credit limit. I didn't open the Sales Order credit-limit code itself. I'm taking that side from your description. What does gate Purchase Order submission is a set of status flags on the supplier. I traced them through `purchase_order.py` and `accounts_controller.py`. **What gates Purchase Order submission** 1. **Supplier on-hold block.** - `AccountsController.ensure_supplier_is_not_blocked()` is in `erpnext/controllers/accounts_controller.py`, around line 153. - It applies to Purchase Order and Purchase Invoice, and to Payment Entry when the party is a supplier. - If `Supplier.on_hold` is set and `hold_type` is "All" or "Invoices", it raises "{supplier} is blocked so this transaction cannot proceed". - It only blocks while `release_date` is empty or today is on or before it. - A hold type of "Payments" blocks only Payment Entry. - The Purchase Order tests `test_po_for_blocked_supplier_all` and `test_po_for_blocked_supplier_invoices` expect a `ValidationError` on creation. - I did not trace which hook calls this method, and I did not read the "Payments" test for Purchase Order. 2. **Supplier scorecard standing.** - `PurchaseOrder.validate_supplier()` is in `erpnext/buying/doctype/purchase_order/purchase_order.py`, around line 272. It is called from `validate()`, around line 200. - If `Supplier.prevent_pos` is set, it throws "Purchase Orders are not allowed for {supplier} due to a scorecard standing of {status}". - If `Supplier.warn_pos` is set, it only shows an orange "Caution" message. - The Supplier Scorecard (`supplier_scorecard.py`) sets these flags, by standing level, onto the Supplier. **How this differs from a credit limit** - **What it measures.** A credit limit is quantitative and financial. It compares the customer's outstanding balance plus the new order value against a monetary threshold. The supplier checks are qualitative and state-based. They test boolean flags: an admin's manual hold, or a scorecard-derived standing. No amount is compared. - **Direction of exposure.** A credit limit protects you from the customer's receivables risk. The supplier checks gate purchasing for performance or administrative reasons. They are not a cap on how much you owe. - **Amount-agnostic.** A Purchase Order of any value passes or fails the same way. - **Hard and soft modes.** The hard block (`prevent_pos` or `on_hold`) throws. The soft mode (`warn_pos`) only warns and does not stop submission. - **Budget control.** The closest thing to a spend limit is the Budget feature, in `erpnext/controllers/budget_controller.py`. It is a separate mechanism against accounts, cost centers and projects, and it is not tied to a supplier.

**Short answer:** No. Purchase Order has no automatic spend-limit check against a supplier. The Supplier doctype has no credit-limit field, and nothing sums outstanding payables or open POs against a cap before submit. **What gates Purchase Order submission instead** 1. **Supplier Scorecard standing.** This is the main gate. - `PurchaseOrder.validate_supplier()` in `erpnext/buying/doctype/purchase_order/purchase_order.py` (around lines 272–294) runs during validation. Validation runs before submit, so a draft that fails can't be submitted. - It reads `Supplier.prevent_pos`. If that is set and the supplier's `Supplier Scorecard` has a `status`, it calls `frappe.throw("Purchase Orders are not allowed for … due to a scorecard standing of …")`. That blocks the save and therefore the submit. - It then reads `Supplier.warn_pos`. If that is set, it shows a non-blocking orange `msgprint` ("Caution"). - The flags come from the scorecard. `SupplierScorecard.validate()` calls `update_standing()` in `supplier_scorecard.py`. That copies `prevent_pos`, `warn_pos`, `prevent_rfqs` and `warn_rfqs` from the matching `Supplier Scorecard Scoring Standing` band onto the Supplier. The default "Very Poor" standing sets `prevent_pos=1`, and "Poor" sets `warn_pos=1`. 2. **Supplier "on hold" is not a Purchase Order gate.** `Supplier.on_hold` and `hold_type` are checked in `erpnext/controllers/accounts_controller.py` (around lines 162–164). The hold types that block are "All", "Invoices" and "Payments". The visible code covers buying invoices and supplier payments, so I wouldn't count it as a PO gate. I did not open that function in full, so I haven't confirmed whether it also applies to Purchase Orders. `test_purchase_order.py` has tests that toggle `supplier.on_hold` (around line 744), but I didn't read them. **How it differs from a credit limit** - **Sales Order credit limit.** `SalesOrder.check_credit_limit()` calls `customer.check_credit_limit(customer, company)`. This is a quantitative, financial check. It compares the customer's outstanding receivables and open orders against a per-company amount stored in `Customer Credit Limit`. It can be bypassed per company with `bypass_credit_limit_check`. It is also re-run in `on_update_after_submit`, and `SalesInvoice.check_credit_limit()` runs a similar check. - **Purchase Order supplier gate.** This is a qualitative, performance-based flag. It depends on the supplier's scorecard standing (a score built from weighted criteria such as delivery and quality), not on how much is owed. A tiny PO is blocked just as a large one is, and a huge PO passes if the standing is good. It also protects the buyer from an unreliable vendor, whereas a credit limit protects the seller from a customer's credit risk. There is no `bypass` field. The only ways around it are to change the scorecard or Supplier flags, or to clear the standing.
